newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia trade deficit forecast to improve in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia trade deficit forecast to improve in 1996.

text.p: Malaysia could post a huge trade deficit in July after two months of surplus, but full-year forecasts have been revised down sharply, economists and analysts said on Wednesday.

In a poll by Reuters, economists from nine research houses said the 1996 trade deficit would be an average 4.95 billion ringgit ($1.98 billion) against an average 8.55 billion ringgit they had predicted three months ago.
This compares with a trade gap of 9.2 billion ringgit last year.
Dealers and economists said the market was expecting a trade deficit of up to one billion ringgit in July.

The head of regional currencies at a Singapore-based European bank said this expectation was gaining strength because of the "unbelievably low (trade) deficit" Malaysia recorded in the first six months of the year.

The economists said the revision in the full-year forecast followed a sharply lower trade deficit of 798.4 million ringgit in the first six months of 1996 against a 5.6 billion gap in the corresponding period last year.
The Reuter poll drew predictions that the 1996 balance of trade figure would range from a seven billion ringgit deficit to a 400 million surplus.
The earlier poll in June included 18 economists from various research houses.

The economists gave varied reasons for the predicted sharp deterioration in the trade balance in the second half of 1996. They included a drop in electronics exports in the second half, higher imports of big equipment and machinery and falling commodity export earnings.

The first half benefited from the ringgit's appreciation against the yen, increased gains from petroleum exports on higher global prices and strong exports of electronic goods despite a worldwide slump, the economists said.

"First, commodity export values came down. Couple that with electronics exports, which will come down, and the lumpy imports expected, they will increase the import number (and widen the deficit in the second half)," said Patrick Er, economist with CIMB Securities in Kuala Lumpur.

He said Malaysian electronic exports were probably sustained by a large backlog of orders in the first half. However, expecting a slowdown, manufacturers had already reduced their imports in the first half. Malaysia imports a high percentage of components for the electronic goods it makes for export.
"In the second half the exports will come down. Imports are already down," he said.
According to Andy Tan, economist with MMS International in Singapore, the trend would seem to suggest dramatic improvement in the trade balance, but that may not be the case in the end.
"The trade deficit will most certainly improve over last year, but it will not be that dramatic. It should be around five billion ringgit," he said.
He said the trade deficit would probably widen in the second half if aircraft, ships and trains are delivered as expected.
Other economists said a drop in the growth of capital goods imports to four percent from 25 percent last year and a surge in oil revenues due to higher prices would help Malaysia's trade account.
